prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Once I believed in you; I planted a fig tree. Here, in Vermont, country of no summer. It was a test: if the tree lived, it would mean you existed. By this logic, you do not exist. Or you exist exclusively in warmer climates, in fervent Sicily and Mexico and California, where are grown the unimaginable apricot and fragile peach. Perhaps they see your face in Sicily; here we barely see the hem of your garment. I have to discipline myself to share with John and Noah the tomato crop. If there is justice in some other world, those like myself, whom nature forces into lives of abstinence, should get the lion's share of all things, all objects of hunger, greed being praise of you. And no one praises more intensely than I, with more painfully checked desire, or more deserves to sit at your right hand, if it exists, partaking of the perishable, the immortal fig, which does not travel.

outputs.L3:
# On Planting Faith in Frozen Ground

There was a time when I believed—truly believed—in a divine presence that moved through the world, attentive and responsive to the small tests we devise to prove its existence. To confirm this belief, I planted a fig tree in Vermont. It seemed a reasonable experiment: if God existed, surely He could coax sweetness from unlikely soil, could bend the rules of climate and season to nurture a Mediterranean fruit in a New England yard. The fig tree became my altar and my question mark all at once.

But Vermont is not kind to fig trees. The winters arrived with their characteristic cruelty, and no amount of hope or prayer could keep the branches from succumbing to frost. The tree withered, and with it, something in my certainty withered too. I concluded, with the strange logic of disappointed faith, that either God does not exist at all, or—if He does—He has chosen to reside elsewhere, in places where the ground stays warm and forgiving: Sicily, perhaps, or Mexico, or California. These are the latitudes where fig trees flourish without struggle, where the divine, if it exists, must surely feel more at home.

This led me to a further speculation: that perhaps proximity to God is a matter of geography and temperature. Those who live beneath warmer suns may walk in closer communion with whatever sacred force governs existence, while those of us in colder climates are left to glimpse only fragments—faint traces of a presence that has settled more fully elsewhere, leaving us with winter and longing instead of ripened fruit.

And yet, I have come to believe that this deprivation is not without its own strange merit. My life here has been one of forced abstinence, of restraint imposed not by choice but by circumstance—by frost, by short summers, by soil that refuses to yield what warmer earth gives freely. Surely such sacrifice deserves compensation. Surely the one who has wanted so long, so persistently, in conditions hostile to wanting, should be granted the richest measure of what is desired when it finally comes within reach.

I would argue, in fact, that my very deprivation is a form of devotion—that the intensity of my longing, sharpened and deepened by every failed harvest, by every fig that never ripened, constitutes the purest praise I could offer. It is easy to worship abundance; it is harder, and perhaps more sacred, to worship absence, to keep faith with a fruit that will not grow. This aching, unfulfilled desire is my liturgy. And if there is any justice in the order of things, it is this: that I, who have suffered the longest drought of figs, should be the one most deserving of communion with the divine—not through some portable, everyday blessing, but through the fig itself, immortal and unmovable, the very thing that cannot be transported to where I am, only reached by finally, impossibly, being where it is.
outputs.L4:
# The Fig Tree

I planted the fig tree in April, when the frost had only just begun to loosen its grip on the Vermont soil, and I told no one what I intended by it. This was to be my experiment, my quiet interrogation of the universe conducted not through prayer or scripture but through horticulture. If God existed—if some benevolent intelligence truly watched over the affairs of small, doubting men—then surely He could sustain one Mediterranean tree through a New England winter. It seemed a fair test, even a merciful one. I was not asking for miracles, only for the ordinary grace extended to olive groves in Tuscany, to fig orchards along the Turkish coast. I was asking, in essence, for proof that required nothing more than the bending of natural law in one small, verifiable instance.

The tree came from a nursery two counties over, a sapling no taller than my forearm, its leaves already curling with the shock of transplantation. I dug the hole myself, working the shovel through soil still hard with the memory of winter, and I remember thinking that this labor was itself a kind of prayer—the only honest kind, perhaps, being action rather than supplication. I mixed compost into the clay-heavy earth. I positioned the tree to catch the southern light. I built a small windbreak from scrap lumber, though I told myself this was merely reasonable horticultural practice, not a hedging of my theological bet.

Through May and June, the tree seemed to answer with tentative hope. New leaves unfurled, pale green and trembling, and I found myself checking on it each morning before coffee, searching its branches for some sign—not of divinity exactly, but of the possibility of divinity, which is perhaps the only sign we are ever granted in this life. By July, small green figs appeared, hard and unripe, and I felt something in my chest loosen that I had not realized was clenched. Perhaps, I thought, the world was kinder than I had assumed. Perhaps proof could be so simple, so quietly botanical.

But Vermont does not forgive presumption. The autumn came early and cruel that year, and by October the leaves had blackened at their edges, curling inward like hands drawing back from a flame. I covered the tree with burlap, then with a makeshift structure of plastic sheeting, but these were the gestures of a man who already suspects the outcome and merely delays its confirmation. The figs, unripened, fell to the frozen ground one by one, small green fists that would never open. By December, the tree itself had gone the color of driftwood, brittle and unmistakably dead.

I did not weep, though I had expected to. Instead I found myself thinking of all the places where such a tree might have thrived without struggle—the terraced hillsides of Calabria, the courtyards of Damascus, anywhere the sun fell generous and constant upon the earth. Perhaps, I thought, divinity was not absent from the world but simply provincial in its mercies, flowing more readily toward lands already blessed with warmth and fertility, leaving harder places to fend for themselves with only the cold comfort of self-reliance. This seemed almost worse than atheism: not the absence of God, but His preferential geography.

Yet as winter deepened and I found myself still returning to that patch of dead earth, unable to quite let go of the small grave I had made, another thought began to take root—one that felt truer than my original hypothesis, though it offered no vindication. I began to understand that perhaps the fig tree's death was never meant to prove or disprove anything at all, but rather to illuminate something about the nature of longing itself. The tree had wanted so desperately to live in a place that could not sustain it. Every leaf it had produced, every fruit it had attempted to ripen, represented not folly but a kind of magnificent, doomed devotion—an insistence on flourishing despite conditions that made flourishing impossible.

I thought then of all the forms of longing that exist under conditions of scarcity: the desert mystic whose faith burns brighter for having so little water to distract him, the exile who loves his homeland with an intensity the native-born can never quite achieve, the dying man who finds in his final months a clarity about existence that health had always obscured. Perhaps it is precisely those who exist in the most restrained circumstances—starved of warmth, of certainty, of the ordinary abundances that make belief easy—who offer up the most fervent, most authentic form of devotion. Not despite their deprivation, but because of it.

The fig tree had asked everything of a climate that could give it nothing, and in that asking, it had performed something almost sacred: a refusal to accept the limitations of its circumstances, even unto death. I began to wonder if this was not, in fact, the truest form of faith available to us—not the comfortable belief of those born into fertile lands where survival requires no particular conviction, but the harder faith of those who plant fig trees in frozen ground, who continue reaching toward warmth they may never feel, who love what cannot be sustained and are made more devoted, not less, by that impossibility.

If there is a God who metes out rewards according to merit, I came to think, He must reserve His greatest tenderness not for the flourishing orchards of gentler climates, but for those solitary, doomed trees that attempt to grow where growing should not be possible—for the quality of longing is not diminished by its lack of fulfillment, but perhaps, paradoxically, made more pure by it. The tree in my backyard died in December, but I have come to suspect that its brief, striving life constituted a more genuine prayer than any I have spoken aloud, precisely because it asked for everything and received nothing, and reached anyway.
outputs.L5:
# Once in Vermont

Once, in the quiet hills of Vermont, autumn arrived like a painter's dream. The maples burned crimson and gold, cascading down the slopes toward valleys where mist clung to the morning air.

Here, time seemed to move differently. Here, the small towns with their white church steeples and covered bridges stood as they had for generations, largely untouched by the rush of modern life. Farmers still tended their dairy herds at dawn, and the scent of maple syrup boiling in sugarhouses drifted across the countryside each spring.

Once you've walked these back roads, once you've watched the sun set behind the Green Mountains, casting long shadows across fields of wildflowers, you understand why so many people fall in love with this small New England state. Vermont doesn't shout for attention—it simply exists in its quiet, unhurried beauty, waiting for those who seek it out.

Whether it's the ski slopes of Stowe in winter, the farmers' markets bursting with local produce in summer, or the spectacular foliage that draws visitors from around the world each fall, Vermont offers something increasingly rare: a genuine connection to the land and the rhythms of the seasons. Here, in this small corner of America, life still moves at the pace of the changing leaves.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the voice of a gardener addressing God with doubt and longing, using a fig tree in Vermont as a test of faith.
counterfactuals.output:
**Overwintering**

You know I planted a fig tree in Vermont,
which is either an act of faith or spite,
I haven't decided which. Some Octobers
I still don't know.

The books all say it can't be done—
frost line too deep, season too short,
this is stone fruit country, apple country,
your own zone-four proof
that some things aren't meant to travel north.

But I dug the hole anyway. I dug it
the way I've dug most things in my life,
without asking whether you'd bless it first.

Every November I bend the trunk down
like a man forcing another man to kneel,
lay it flat along the ground I've softened,
and bury it—all six feet of green ambition—
under leaves, under a tarp, under snow
that will come whether I'm ready or not.

I don't know why I do this to something
that only wants to reach for light.
I don't know why you'd make a tree
that wants the Mediterranean
and drop its seed in a mind like mine,
stubborn, half-believing, up here
where the sun leaves by four
and doesn't apologize.

Some years I dig it up in April
and it's black inside, mush and rot,
a lesson I should have learned already
about what this soil will and won't allow.

Other years—and this is the part
I can't explain to anyone who hasn't done it—
other years there's a green thumb of growth
pushing through what looked like death,
and I stand there in my mud boots
not shouting hallelujah exactly
but close to it. Close enough
that the neighbors probably wonder.

I want to ask you something
I'm not sure has an answer:
is this what you meant by faith—
this annual burial, this refusal
to let a thing die
even when the ground says otherwise?

Or am I just stubborn
in a way that looks like belief
if you squint?

I don't need the figs, particularly.
They come small and strange up here anyway,
never quite what the catalog promised.
It's the digging I can't give up,
the bending of green wood in October light,
the going down on my knees each fall
into the actual dirt
to save something
that has no business surviving
this far north
of where you supposedly
made it grow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Louise Glück–style poem titled "Vespers," blending religious address with images of fruit, climate, and denial.
counterfactuals.output:
Vespers

In your extended absence, you permit me
use of earth, expecting
in return some tenderness toward the fruit
you do not eat, the pear trees
heavy and confused,
bearing too much, too early—

I tell myself this is the season's error,
not yours, not mine. The climate
has changed. Everyone says so, standing
in gardens grown suddenly
foreign, the light
falling differently on the same dirt.

I do not think you punish us.
I think you have simply stopped looking,
the way I have stopped looking
at what I no longer want to see:
the bruised side of the apple,
the wasp already inside it.

Ask me what I believe and I will tell you
nothing has died here that wanted to live.
That the drought is only weather.
That the fruit drops because it is heavy,
not because something has withdrawn its hand.

You are the ripening I refuse to name.
I go on watering what's already rotting,
calling it faith, calling it patience—
as if tenderness were not another way
of turning from the truth:

that the orchard was never yours or mine,
that what we tend, we tend toward ending,
and the sweetness, when it comes,
comes already leaving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem where the speaker questions divine existence through failed cultivation of a fig tree, contrasting cold New England with fertile Mediterranean lands.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Fig Tree's Silence

I planted it against the northern wall,
where morning light might linger longest,
this transplant from some warmer myth—
a fig tree in New England, foolish hope
wrapped in burlap through October's warning frost.

They say in Sicily the branches bend
with fruit so heavy children pick them
without reaching, that the soil itself
seems generous there, complicit
in some ancient bargain no one
had to speak aloud. The sun
does half the praying.

Here I mulch and wrap and pray
in whatever language failing gardeners use—
not quite belief, not quite abandonment,
somewhere in the frozen middle
where the doubtful kneel.

Three years the leaves came green and hopeful,
spread like hands in supplication,
and three years the fruit stayed hard and small,
green knuckles that would not ripen,
would not soften into sweetness
no matter how I turned them toward the light.

If there is a gardener behind all gardens,
why plant such longing in a northern climate?
Why give the fig tree's shape and shade
to soil that keeps its own cold counsel,
that freezes six months out of twelve?

Perhaps the Mediterranean sun
knows something about grace
that New England frost has never learned—
that some are born to ripen easily
and some must break themselves
against a granite winter, calling
into air that doesn't answer,
tending trees that won't bear fruit,
and calling *that* devotion,
calling that a kind of faith:

to keep on watering
the barren ground,
to keep on speaking
to the silent dirt,
to love the tree
that will not love you back
with fruit, with sweetness,
with the affirmation
that the digging
and the waiting
meant anything at all.

I have unwrapped the burlap every spring
to find the same stunted argument,
the same small green fists
refusing to open into yes.

Maybe God is like New England weather—
present in the cold that shapes us,
absent in the way that matters,
the way that would mean
figs by August, sweetness
without struggle, proof
that someone, somewhere,
intended this to work.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short lyrical poem about faith, deprivation, and desire, using gardening and fruit imagery as metaphors for belief in God.
counterfactuals.output:
# Orchard of Waiting

I planted faith in barren ground,
Not knowing what would come—
A seed of doubt, a want unbound,
My hands grew rough and numb.

The soil cracked beneath the sun,
No rain for many a year,
Yet still I dug, my labor done
In hunger, not in fear.

For deprivation taught me this:
The root grows deep in drought,
And what the empty hand may miss,
The starving heart cries out.

I dreamed of apples, dark and sweet,
Of figs upon the vine,
The taste I've never known to eat—
A hunger half-divine.

Is this belief, this reaching hand
Toward fruit I cannot see?
Perhaps to thirst is to understand
What blooms eventually.

So I will tend this barren row,
Believe in branch and stem,
Though I may never live to know
If God grows there—or them.

The gardener kneels in soil unkind,
Desire her only tool—
Faith is the fruit that stays behind
The reaching, patient, fool.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a monologue-style poem addressing "you" (God), exploring bitterness over unanswered prayers and unfulfilled abundance, set in a Vermont garden with mentions of John and Noah.
counterfactuals.output:
**Late August, Talking to the Dirt**

You said abundance, and I believed you,
planted the tomatoes in rows like prayers,
staked them with old broom handles
because that's what we had, that's what
you gave us to work with in this
Vermont clay that cracks
under a sun you also made.

I want to ask you plainly:
where were you in June
when the frost took the beans
after I'd already thinned them twice,
already thanked you for the thinning?

John says trust the process.
John says the mountains don't move
because they weren't meant to,
that stillness is its own answer.
But John has never watched
a whole row of squash blossoms
drop before they fruited,
watched them fall like
something you decided
not to finish saying.

Noah doesn't pray anymore.
He says the garden taught him that—
says if you were listening
the drought wouldn't have lasted
three Augusts running,
says the well runs dry
regardless of how good
we've tried to be.

I don't disagree with him
so much as I keep coming back
to this dirt anyway,
kneeling in it like it might
still answer for you,
like the worms turning it over
are some kind of language
I haven't learned to read.

You could have sent rain.
You could have made the beetles
choose another garden,
could have let the pole beans climb
the way I imagined them climbing
when I sowed them with such
stupid, stubborn hope.

Instead: the deer got the lettuce.
Instead: the hail in July.
Instead: this half-empty basket
I'm bringing in at dusk
while the light goes that particular gold
that Vermont does so well,
so cruelly well,
like beauty was never
the thing that was promised.

I keep asking anyway.
Not because I think you'll answer
but because the asking
is its own small plot of ground,
because Noah's silence
and John's stillness
aren't enough to live on,
because somewhere in me
there's still a seed
that hasn't figured out
it isn't going to grow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
